Proposition 1 : $11.25 billion state housing bond
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 1 would let the state borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds for housing. About $10 billion would go to state housing programs, mostly for building and renovating affordable rental housing, plus homebuyer help, farmworker, tribal and student housing, and housing infrastructure. The other $1.25 billion would fund home loans for veterans.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 1 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 1
Borrowing $10 billion for housing programs, repaid from the state General Fund, plus $1.25 billion for veterans' home loans, repaid by borrowers
Cost to repay $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years (Legislative Analyst)
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's final vote Assembly 61-7, Senate 29-2 (June 25, 2026)
Money raised, Jan. 1 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $16.42 million (three committees, net of transfers). Against: no committee reported
Largest donors Airbnb, Building a Better California, and the Western States and North Coast States regional councils of carpenters, $1 million each
Outside spending Against: $40,500 by Reform California (slate mailers and door hangers shared with other props). For: about $312,000
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 60% yes, 38% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are from the committees' state campaign filings in the Secretary of State's Cal-Access database.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , The details , How it got on the ballot , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 1 mean?
The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 1 mean?
The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
What would Proposition 1 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would pay $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years to repay the $10 billion housing bond, about 0.25% of the state General Fund budget. The $1.25 billion veterans bond would be repaid by veterans' loan payments, which the Analyst says has always meant no direct state cost.
What it means for the City of LA
The City of Los Angeles would not receive a set share. The money goes through state competitive programs, mostly loans to developers and local governments for affordable rental housing. $200 million is set aside for local housing trust funds and local pilot programs. A 2026 Enterprise Community Partners study counted 9,533 stalled affordable homes in Los Angeles and Ventura counties waiting for public funding. The state would repay the bond from its General Fund, not from City taxes.
The details
Official title Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Type Legislative statute (general obligation bond), placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. The State Constitution (Article XVI, Section 1) says a state bond law takes effect only if it receives "a majority of all the votes cast for and against it."
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond. Supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 1 on the March 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for mental health treatment facilities, which passed with 50.2% of the vote (Secretary of State, March 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 1 passes
State housing bond money The 2018 housing bond has been spent. The last voter-approved housing money was $2 billion in the 2024 mental health bond (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm); LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)) $10 billion in new general obligation bonds for housing programs (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Veterans home loans (CalVet) Last funded by a $1 billion bond in 2018 (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)) $1.25 billion more, repaid by veterans’ mortgage payments (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
State budget About $6 billion a year goes to repay bonds, about 3% of General Fund revenue (LAO bond overview (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf#page=80)) $500 million to $600 million more a year for about 25 years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Recent state spending on these programs The 2026 Budget Act gives $500 million for state low-income housing tax credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, the California Budget & Policy Center says (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)) Bond money would be added to these programs over several years (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm))
Changes to how the money is split Not applicable The Legislature may move money among the listed programs “as necessary to effectively promote the development of affordable housing” (text, Sec. 54056 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2))
Reporting Not applicable The state housing department must publish an annual report on what the bond paid for (text, Sec. 54088 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Where the $10 billion would go (text, Sec. 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)):
Program Amount
Multifamily Housing Program (rental housing; at least 10% of assisted units for extremely low income households) $5.1 billion
Supportive housing through the Multifamily Housing Program, including $150 million for youth housing $1.15 billion
Portfolio Reinvestment Program (keeping existing state-funded rentals affordable) $750 million
CalHome (homeownership and self-help housing) $600 million
CalHFA home purchase (down payment) assistance $500 million
Infill Infrastructure Grant Program $500 million
Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing $450 million
Student housing, split between UC and CSU $350 million
Buying existing unrestricted housing and adding affordability limits $200 million
Tribal Housing Grant Program $200 million
Local housing trust funds and local pilot programs (Affordable Housing Innovation Fund) $200 million
Source: Proposition 1 text, Section 54054 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1). The separate $1.25 billion veterans bond is in the Military and Veterans Code section of the same text (text, Sec. 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)).
The Legislative Analyst estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental apartments, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds. It would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, buy or repair homes (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The measure sets no production targets of its own (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
No set share for the City. The bond money goes to state programs. The Legislative Analyst says the rental programs “generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Projects in Los Angeles would compete for it statewide. The analysis does not estimate how much would reach the City.
Money cities can apply for. $200 million would be “available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). The text sends it through the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program, which requires a local trust fund with its own ongoing money (text, Sec. 54054(b)(11) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=2)).
Stalled projects in the region. Enterprise Community Partners, a nonprofit housing lender that backs Proposition 1 and gave $100,000 to the Yes campaign, counted 39,880 affordable homes statewide that had local approvals but lacked the funding to start construction at the end of 2025. It put 9,533 of them in Los Angeles and Ventura counties. It did not break out the City of Los Angeles (Enterprise report, p. 3 (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2026-03/2026_State_Pipeline_Brief.pdf#page=3); Yes on Prop 1 coalition list (https://yesonprop1ca.com/coalition)).
The City’s own housing tax. The City’s main local source of new affordable housing money is Measure ULA, the tax on property sales over $5 million. The Housing Department reported it raised nearly $1.2 billion from its start through April 30, 2026 (LAHD report, May 10, 2026 (https://cityclerk.lacity.org/onlinedocs/2026/26-0088-S1_rpt_lahd_05-10-26.pdf)). The Legislative Analyst says Proposition 1 money “would be used together with other government monies” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)).
No City tax. The state would repay the $10 billion bond from its General Fund (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). Proposition 1 does not create a local tax (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
We did not find a City Council resolution or City Housing Department statement on Proposition 1 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Proposition 1 is a bond act written by the Legislature. It needed a two-thirds vote in each house and the Governor’s signature, then voter approval (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI); SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Feb. 18, 2025: SB 417 was introduced (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). Its lead authors are Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas. The principal coauthors are Sen. Christopher Cabaldon and Assemblymember Buffy Wicks (SB 417 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 6, 2026: The Senate Housing Committee approved it 8-1 (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Jan. 27, 2026: The Senate passed it 30-9. The no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Choi, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Niello, Seyarto, Strickland and Valladares (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
April 22 and May 14, 2026: The Assembly Housing Committee (10-2) and Appropriations Committee (12-3) approved it (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
June 25, 2026: The Assembly passed the amended bill 61-7, the Senate agreed 29-2, and Gov. Gavin Newsom signed it the same day. It became Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026 (SB 417 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)). The Assembly no votes were Chen, DeMaio, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Seyarto and Strickland (SB 417 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a state bond law cannot take effect until it has been submitted to the people and “shall have received a majority of all the votes cast for and against it at such election” (Cal. Const. art. XVI, sec. 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&division=&title=&part=&chapter=&article=XVI)). The bond act itself says it becomes operative only if voters adopt it on Nov. 3, 2026 (text, Sec. 54051 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=1)).
Related past measures.
Proposition 1 (November 2018): a $4 billion housing and veterans bond (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 56.2% statewide and 64.4% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)). The Budget Center says its money was fully committed by the end of 2023 (Budget Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/)).
Proposition 2 (November 2018): $2 billion for supportive housing for people with mental illness (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)). It passed with 63.4% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2018 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/92-ballot-measures.pdf)).
Proposition 1 (March 2024): a mental health bond that included $2 billion for housing for veterans and others facing homelessness (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)). It passed with 50.2% statewide and 54.0% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, March 2024 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/sov/115-state-ballot-measures-formatted.pdf)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
The argument in favor is signed by Anni Chung of Self-Help for the Elderly, Jeffery Freitas of the California Federation of Teachers and John H. Ing of US Vets (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Need: “More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.”
Veterans: $1.25 billion goes “solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership” through CalVet.
Construction: it “jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes.”
Taxes and oversight: “NO NEW TAXES,” with public reporting, and it “unlocks federal matching funds.”
No argument against Proposition 1 was submitted, so there are no rebuttals (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Chione Flegal, executive director of Housing California, which backs the measure, told the Bay Area News Group that tens of thousands of affordable units are “shovel-ready” and that “you have both an incredible need and the conditions to actually get building quickly” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says “the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest” and that bonds used for programs rather than capital projects are “a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget” (HJTA 2026 voting guide (https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/)). Spokesperson Susan Shelley said, “The more you pile this debt on, the more difficult the budget process is” (Bay Area News Group via Press Democrat (https://www.pressdemocrat.com/2026/09/21/housing-ballot-measure-california-election/)).
State Sen. Tony Strickland, who voted no, told LAist the measure has a “noble goal” but could end up “bankrupting our next generation,” and said, “We could definitely find $10 billion within the general fund spending, and within our normal budget, without doing bond indebtedness” (LAist (https://laist.com/news/politics/voter-guides/laist-california-voter-game-plan-proposition-prop-1-november-2026-election-guide)).
California YIMBY supports it and estimates the production money could build about 43,700 affordable homes. It also says the $500 million in down payment help “could drive up home prices” if housing supply does not grow (California YIMBY (https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-1-2026/)).

The state would repay the $10 billion bond from the General Fund at $500 million to $600 million a year, about 0.25% of the General Fund budget (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm)).
